posts.title: Building a theme system with CSS variables in Next.js
posts.excerpt: How to build a flexible multi-theme system using CSS custom properties and React context — no libraries required.

body.content: CSS custom properties (variables) are the most underrated tool in a frontend developer's arsenal. Combined with React context, they let you build a theme system that is fast, flexible, and requires zero runtime overhead.
Why not a library?

Libraries like Styled-Components, Emotion, or even Stitches add kilobytes of runtime JavaScript to solve a problem that CSS already solves natively. CSS variables update instantly, cascade correctly, and work with any styling approach — Tailwind, CSS Modules, inline styles, whatever you prefer.
The structure
The system has three layers: design tokens as CSS variables on :root, a theme map in TypeScript, and a React context that applies the chosen theme's values to the DOM.
The React context

The ThemeProvider reads localStorage on mount, applies the chosen theme's variables directly to document.documentElement, and exposes setTheme and toggleMode to child components. No re-renders required for color changes — the CSS variable update handles everything.
Multiple themes, same system

Because every color in the UI reads from a CSS variable, adding a new theme is just adding a new object to the theme map. No component changes needed. This is the power of separating data from presentation.
The best theme system is the one you forget is there — it just works, for every theme, everywhere.
Performance
CSS variable updates happen in a single paint. No JavaScript reconciliation. No virtual DOM diffing. The browser handles it natively. This is why theme switching feels instant — because it is.

content: No flicker on initial load when using localStorage + SSR
Works with Tailwind's dark: variant via the .dark class
Each theme can override any subset of variables

posts.title: GSAP scroll animations that actually feel good
posts.excerpt: Practical patterns for smooth, purposeful scroll-triggered animations in React without over-engineering.

body.content: Most scroll animations I see on portfolios fall into one of two traps: either they're so subtle you barely notice them, or they're so aggressive that the page feels broken. Good scroll animation has one job: direct attention to what matters, when it matters.
The golden rule
Animate things that benefit from animation. A heading appearing as you scroll to it is meaningful — the motion reinforces that this content is new. A button spinning on hover is noise.
Setting up GSAP with React
The critical thing in React is using gsap.context() to scope your animations and calling ctx.revert() on cleanup. This prevents memory leaks and stale animation state on route changes.
Easing matters more than duration
expo.out is your best friend. It starts fast and decelerates naturally — the way physical objects actually move. A 0.7s expo.out feels snappier than a 0.3s linear animation.
Duration is how long. Easing is how it feels. Get the easing right and the duration barely matters.

posts.title: Node.js API architecture for 2024
posts.excerpt: Rate limiting, structured error handling, input validation, and logging patterns I use in every production API.

body.content: I've built Node.js APIs for startups, agencies, and solo projects. After enough production incidents, you develop opinions. These are mine — battle-tested patterns that I now apply from day one.
Structured error handling
Every API error should have a machine-readable code, a human-readable message, and an HTTP status. Never throw raw Error objects — create an AppError class that serializes cleanly.
Input validation at the boundary

Validate every request before it touches business logic. I use Zod because it gives you TypeScript types for free from the same schema definition. The parse happens in middleware — if it fails, a 400 is returned automatically.
Rate limiting is not optional

express-rate-limit with a Redis store. Different limits for different routes — auth endpoints get stricter limits than read-only data endpoints. Apply it globally with a more generous default, then tighten specific routes.

content: Separate limits for authenticated vs anonymous

body.content: Your API is only as reliable as its weakest boundary. Most attacks target the boundary.

projects.title: Clipper
projects.desc: AI content OS for clipper creators — a campaign brief becomes ideas, a plan, clips, and performance feedback in one loop.
projects.summary: One workspace for short-form creators who clip brand campaigns: campaign analysis, content ideas, planner, production, clip maker, library, and analytics — with the AI closing the loop back into ideas.
projects.challenge: Clipper work scatters across notes, a spreadsheet, a clipping tool, and platform analytics. Every stage loses the context of the one before it, so the AI has nothing to learn from.
projects.solution: Nine screens on one data model, so each stage writes what the next one reads: campaign → analysis → ideas → planner → production → clips → library → analytics → optimisation. Next.js App Router, Prisma on libSQL/Turso, NextAuth for sessions, and the Vercel AI SDK for the analysis and optimisation steps.
projects.outcome: The loop is the product. Analytics feeds ideas directly, so the workspace gets sharper with every campaign instead of starting from zero.

projects.title: BOS
projects.desc: Two apps in one repo — a NestJS REST API and a Next.js frontend, kept on the same conventions.
projects.summary: A monorepo split into backend/ and frontend/: NestJS with RxJS and Jest on one side, Next.js with Tailwind on the other, one lint and format standard over both.
projects.challenge: Keeping an API and its client in separate repos meant two pull requests and a version dance for every contract change.
projects.solution: One repo, two apps. NestJS modules with DTO validation and Jest for the API; Next.js App Router with Tailwind and strict TypeScript for the UI. ESLint and Prettier run in both, so a change can't land half-formatted.
projects.outcome: A contract change is one commit — the API and the screen that calls it move together.

projects.title: Chat Group
projects.desc: Realtime group chat — rooms, presence, and message history over Socket.io, with JWT auth and a Postgres store.
projects.summary: Fullstack realtime chat: a Next.js client with Redux Toolkit and Chakra UI, Express + Prisma + PostgreSQL behind it, and Socket.io carrying messages both ways.
projects.challenge: Chat is the classic place where optimistic UI and a real database disagree — the message you see and the message stored aren't always the same one.
projects.solution: Socket.io for transport, Prisma + PostgreSQL as the single source of truth, JWT for auth and bcrypt for credentials. Redux Toolkit with redux-persist keeps the client session across reloads; the server event is what actually appends a message.
projects.outcome: Messages survive a refresh, because the server write — not the client state — is the record.

projects.title: Articles
projects.desc: Blog platform with a rich-text editor, drafts, favourites, and per-user profiles — NextAuth over Prisma.
projects.summary: A publishing app: write in a TipTap editor, keep drafts, publish, favourite what you read, and own a profile.
projects.challenge: Rich text has two failure modes — storing HTML you can't safely render later, or storing JSON you can't search.
projects.solution: TipTap on top of StarterKit for authoring, NextAuth with the Prisma adapter for sessions, Prisma + PostgreSQL for content, Chakra UI for the interface. Posts and profiles stay ordinary rows, so the editor never leaks into the data layer.
projects.outcome: Editing is the hard part, and it lives in one component — everywhere else a post is just text.

projects.title: This Portfolio
projects.desc: This site — editorial layout, multi-theme system, GSAP scroll animations, and a SQLite-backed admin.
projects.summary: The site you're reading: a Next.js App Router portfolio with a theme system, scroll animations, and content you edit from /admin.
projects.challenge: A portfolio you can't update stops being true. Hardcoded content means every new project is a code change and a deploy.
projects.solution: Content lives in SQLite through node:sqlite — no extra service to run — behind route handlers and an admin UI for posts, projects, and photo uploads. Theming is CSS variables driven by a small React context, and GSAP handles the scroll work.
projects.outcome: Adding a project or a post is a form, not a commit.

projects.title: Median API
projects.desc: REST API for a Medium-style publishing backend — JWT auth, DTO validation, and generated Swagger docs.
projects.summary: A NestJS service split into modules with Prisma over PostgreSQL, passport-jwt for auth, and class-validator guarding every payload.
projects.challenge: A REST API without a published contract is a guess — the client finds out what the server accepts by getting a 400 back.
projects.solution: DTOs with class-validator and class-transformer on every route, @nestjs/swagger generating the spec from those same types, Prisma for schema and migrations, and a JWT strategy for protected routes.
projects.outcome: The docs are generated from the validation rules, so they can't drift from what the API actually accepts.

projects.title: Quiz App
projects.desc: Frontend quiz — pick a subject, answer timed questions, and get a scored breakdown at the end.
projects.summary: A quiz flow from subject picker to results: progress, scoring, and a bit of confetti when you land it.
projects.challenge: A quiz is mostly state — current question, selected answer, score, and whether you've already submitted. Get that wrong and a double click scores twice.
projects.solution: A single client-side state machine for the flow, Radix primitives for the answer options and the progress bar, Framer Motion for the transitions, and next-themes for the dark mode toggle.
projects.outcome: Answer → feedback → next question, with no way to submit the same question twice.

projects.title: REST Countries
projects.desc: Country explorer on the REST Countries API — search, region filter, and detail pages you can walk by border.
projects.summary: Browse every country, filter by region or name, then follow a border straight to the next one.
projects.challenge: The API gives you country names for borders, not the countries — so every detail page needs a second lookup just to render its neighbours.
projects.solution: Next.js pages over the REST Countries API, Tailwind for the responsive grid, and a small mapping step that resolves border codes against the full list before render.
projects.outcome: You can travel the map by border instead of going back to the index every time.

projects.title: IP Address Tracker
projects.desc: IP and domain tracker — look up any address, drop it on a Leaflet map, and see the ISP behind it.
projects.summary: Type an IP or a domain, get location, timezone, and ISP, plotted on a live map.
projects.challenge: Map libraries assume they own the layout and the DOM. Leaflet inside React needs its lifecycle handled, and its default marker icons break under a bundler.
projects.solution: react-leaflet with the default-icon fix applied, a controlled form via react-hook-form, and SWR for the lookup so repeat queries come from cache. Map position is state, not a remount.
projects.outcome: A new search re-centres the map instead of rebuilding it.

projects.title: Job Listing
projects.desc: Job board where the filter bar is the whole interface — stack tags narrow the list live.
projects.summary: Search roles by language, tool, or level, and watch the list react as tags come and go.
projects.challenge: Filtering by several tags at once is a set intersection, and doing it in the wrong place means either a request per click or a list that quietly goes stale.
projects.solution: TypeScript with a typed listing shape, the dataset held client-side, and the active filters as a set — so adding a tag is one intersection over an array that's already in memory.
projects.outcome: Every filter change is instant: no request, no spinner.

projects.title: Dictionary
projects.desc: Dictionary lookup — definitions, phonetics, synonyms, and audio pronunciation from one search.
projects.summary: Search a word, get its meanings by part of speech, plus synonyms and a play button for the audio.
projects.challenge: Dictionary responses are nested and irregular: not every entry has phonetics, audio, or synonyms, so naive rendering crashes on the gaps.
projects.solution: Redux Toolkit for search state and the loading/error paths, Axios for the fetch, Chakra UI for the presentation, and defensive rendering that skips missing fields rather than assuming them.
projects.outcome: A word with half the usual fields still renders — the missing parts just don't appear.

projects.title: GitHub User Search
projects.desc: GitHub user search in Vue 3 — profile, repos, followers, and links, in light and dark.
projects.summary: Search a handle and get the profile: avatar, bio, stats, links, and repos.
projects.challenge: Search-as-you-type against a rate-limited API will get you blocked, and an empty state is easy to forget until someone types nonsense.
projects.solution: Vue 3 with Pinia for the store and Vue Router for the profile route, Axios against the GitHub API, and a debounced query with explicit idle / loading / error / empty states. Vitest and Cypress cover the store and the search flow.
projects.outcome: Bad input gets an empty state, not a blank screen.
